newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Burma refugees fall sick in Bangladesh hunger strike.
newsitem.headline: Burma refugees fall sick in Bangladesh hunger strike.

text.p: Scores of Burmese Moslem refugees have fallen ill after activists enforced a mass hunger strike in their camps in southeast Bangladesh, relief officials said on Monday.
A United Nations relief agency official said efforts for a meeting between Bangladeshi officials and militant Burmese refugees were continuing as refugees were starving.
"The situation is unchanged and refugees are starving," Van To Nguyen, chief of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) at Cox's Bazar, told Reuters.

Van To Nguyen said a "tripartite meeting was expected on Tuesday between UNHCR, Bangladesh officials and refugee leaders to inform the agitating refugees that the government has pledged not to send (back) anyone forcibly".
He hoped Tuesday's meeting would break the stalemate and the refugees would end a week-long food strike.

"These people became sick because they had not taken food rations provided by the government for a week. They have been subjected to a mass starvation by their own people," one non-government organisation official told Reuters.
Government officials said they were trying to meet militant leaders to try to persuade them to end the strike.

"If the situation does not improve soon, maybe people will die from starvation. The good news is that nothing has happened yet and we are expecting to avert the worst," one relief official said on Monday.

The food boycott began on July 20 following clashes between police and so-called "Rohingya" refugees at Nayapara camp in Cox's Bazar district over alleged attempts to send them home to Burma forcibly.
The Rohingyas are the remnants of scores of thousands of Burmese Moslems who fled neighbouring Burma to escape what they termed relentless persecution by Burmese authorities.
Authorities postponed the repatriation process indefinitely to contain violence after nearly 20 people were injured in the fighting.
UNHCR lodged a strong protest with the Bangladeshi government over what it called the "forcible repatriation".
Officials on Monday said they had already made preliminary contact with the militants at Nayapara but there was no immediate breakthrough to end the food boycott.
They said three officials led by Relief and Repatriation Commissioner Quamrul Huda were allowed to enter the camp on Sunday evening.
Huda assured the refugees that none would be forced to go back against their will.
"This had slightly eased tension at Nayapara and the other camp at Kutupalong, and maybe they will accept rations soon," one official in Cox's Bazar said.
Huda was on his way to Nayapara again on Monday evening, one official told Reuters in Chittagong by telephone.
